title: Design a CAN Sensor Node — Real-Time Embedded Systems Capstone (S32K, CAN Bus, Watchdog)
description:
This is the Level 1 capstone of the S32K Mastery Path, walked through step by step: a real automotive-style CAN sensor node built on a hard 10-millisecond cooperative scheduler. We go through the precise requirement, the tick-driven architecture, the exact bit layout of both CAN frames (a 0x310 status frame out and a 0x311 command frame in), the INIT-safe-state-first state machine, the non-blocking main loop, the individual task functions for sensing, transmitting, receiving, and driving PWM with slew limiting, a full bench-test plan using a real CAN adapter, and the lesson's own closing question — an unguarded race between the CAN RX callback and the main loop's read of the shared command variable. Every line of code and every bit-table value shown is pulled directly from the capstone lesson; nothing invented, nothing skipped.

Lessons covered in this video:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/s32k-mastery-path/level-1/10-capstone-can-sensor-node/

beats.narration: This is the Level 1 capstone of the S32K Mastery Path, and it's the real thing: a CAN sensor node running on a 10-millisecond real-time schedule, transmitting a live status frame, accepting commands over the bus, and enforcing a genuine safety timeout in firmware. We're going to walk it step by step -- the requirement, the architecture, the exact CAN bit layout, the state machine, the code, the bench-test plan, and a race condition the lesson itself leaves you to solve.

display.heading: Capstone: Design a CAN Sensor Node

beats.narration: Here's the spec, stated precisely, the way a real requirements document would: sample a temperature sensor over ADC every 10 milliseconds, filter it and run plausibility checks, transmit a CAN frame with a defined signal layout every 100 milliseconds including a validity flag and an alive counter, receive a command frame that sets a target PWM duty, drive that PWM output toward the target with safe clamping, and feed a watchdog -- but only when every task reports healthy.

display.heading: The Requirement, Restated Precisely
display.subheading: Six real-time obligations, one firmware image

beats.narration: Everything in this node hangs off a single 10-millisecond hardware tick from the LPIT timer -- the same cooperative-scheduler pattern from the timers and PWM module, now carrying a real payload. The sensor task, the command-watch task, and the output task all run on every tick; the CAN status transmit only runs on every tenth tick, giving you the 100-millisecond cadence without a second timer.

display.heading: Architecture: One Tick Drives Everything
display.subheading: 10 ms cooperative scheduler, 100 ms CAN cadence

beats.narration: This is the actual data flow: ADC into the sensor task, into a shared app_state struct holding temperature, validity, the alive counter, and the PWM target. The CAN transmit task reads that state out to the bus every hundred milliseconds, a CAN receive path writes commands back into it, the output task drives the PWM peripheral, and only if sensor, command, and output health are all true does the loop feed the watchdog.

beats.narration: Now the part that makes this a real vehicle network node, not a toy: the exact bit layout of both CAN frames. Get this table wrong in a real vehicle program and you don't get a compiler error -- you get a bus full of nodes silently misinterpreting each other's bytes.

The status frame, ID 0x310, goes out every 100 milliseconds on 8 bytes: bits 0 to 15 carry CoolantTemp as a signed 16-bit value scaled by 0.1 degrees Celsius, bits 16 to 31 carry SupplyVoltage in millivolts, bit 32 is a SensorValid flag straight from the plausibility check, and bits 36 to 39 are a 4-bit AliveCounter that wraps 0 through 15 -- the receiver's proof that this node hasn't frozen and is re-sending stale bytes.

display.code:
Status frame — ID 0x310, node -> bus, every 100 ms, DLC 8

Bits    Signal          Type     Scale/Offset       Range              Notes
0-15    CoolantTemp     int16    0.1 C, offset 0     -40.0..150.0 C     From module 6's NTC lookup
16-31   SupplyVoltage   uint16   1 mV                0..20000 mV        Node's own rail health
32      SensorValid     bool     -                   0/1                Plausibility result
33      WatchdogOK      bool     -                   0/1                Set 0 the tick before a deliberate non-feed
36-39   AliveCounter    uint4    -                   0..15, wraps       Increments every transmission
40-47   PwmActualPct    uint8    1%                  0..100             What the node is actually driving

beats.narration: The command frame, ID 0x311, comes in from the bus: byte 0 is PwmTargetPct, 0 to 100 percent, and bits 8 to 11 are the sender's own CmdAliveCounter. And here's the safety-critical line in the spec: the node treats that command as stale after 300 milliseconds without a new alive-counter value -- three missed 100-millisecond cycles -- and falls back to a safe state. That one sentence is the whole reason this capstone is interesting.

display.code:
Command frame — ID 0x311, bus -> node, DLC 8

Bits    Signal            Type     Scale/Offset   Range      Notes
0-7     PwmTargetPct      uint8    1%             0..100     Desired output
8-11    CmdAliveCounter   uint4    -              0..15      Sender's alive counter

Rule: command is stale after 300 ms without a new CmdAliveCounter
value (3 missed 100 ms cycles) -> fall back to the safe state.

beats.narration: The state machine makes that safe-state rule concrete. INIT runs once: clocks, pins, ADC, CAN, and timers come up, and outputs are forced to the safe state before any of that -- PWM at zero percent -- so there's no window where an uninitialized peripheral could drive something. Only after that does the tick start driving tasks.

display.heading: State Machine
display.subheading: INIT forces safe state before anything else runs

beats.narration: From NORMAL, three consecutive implausible sensor samples drop the node into FAULT, forcing output to zero percent; it takes five stable samples to earn its way back. And separately, if the command goes stale past 300 milliseconds, the node enters CMD_STALE and holds the last known-good target, clamped -- a distinct failure mode from a sensor fault, with its own recovery path.

power-on
           │
           ▼
     ┌───────────┐   sensor implausible          ┌────────────┐
     │   INIT    │──────────────────────────────▶│   FAULT    │
     └─────┬─────┘   3+ consecutive samples       └─────┬──────┘
           │ clocks/pins/adc/can/timers OK               │ output = safe
           ▼                                              │ (PWM = 0%)
     ┌───────────┐   sensor valid again (5 stable)        │
     │  NORMAL   │◀────────────────────────────────────────┘
     └─────┬─────┘
           │ command stale > 300 ms
           ▼
     ┌───────────┐
     │ CMD_STALE │  PWM holds last-known-good target, clamped;
     └───────────┘  status frame's WatchdogOK-style visibility

beats.narration: Here's the main loop that actually implements that schedule in C. Notice what it does not do: it doesn't block, it doesn't call delay functions, it just checks whether the tick counter has advanced since last time through the loop, and if it has, it runs exactly one 10-millisecond slice of work.

display.heading: Main-Loop Pseudocode
display.subheading: A non-blocking scheduler off one tick counter

beats.narration: app_state_t is the single struct every task reads and writes -- temperature, validity, PWM target and actual, and the command's alive tracking. main forces outputs safe before init even finishes, then loops forever: each new tick runs sensor, command-watch, and output tasks, every tenth tick also transmits the CAN status frame, and the watchdog only gets fed if sensor, command, and output all came back healthy on that same tick.

command_watch_task_10ms is where the 300-millisecond timeout actually lives. If the RX handler updated the alive counter this tick, it resets the age counter to zero and adopts the new target, clamped to 0 through 100. If not, it increments that age counter, and once it passes 30 ticks -- 30 times 10 milliseconds is 300 milliseconds -- it forces the PWM target to zero and reports itself unhealthy. That's the module 7 signal-timeout habit, made concrete in one function.
Now the actual task implementations. Three functions, each one owning exactly one responsibility, each one returning a bool the main loop uses to decide whether it's safe to feed the watchdog.

sensor_task_10ms reads the ADC channel; if the raw value falls outside the plausible range, it counts consecutive faults and only marks the reading invalid after more than five in a row -- so one noisy sample doesn't trip a fault, but a genuinely dead sensor does. Otherwise it resets the fault counter and runs the reading through the NTC lookup and filter from the ADC module.

can_tx_status_task_100ms packs temperature and voltage into little-endian bytes, and packs the valid flag and the incrementing alive counter into a single byte using a bitmask and shift, exactly matching the bit table from earlier. And can_on_command_received -- the RX callback -- rejects any target above 100 percent outright, then writes the new target and alive value into globals and sets a flag the command-watch task consumes on its next pass.

output_task_10ms is the last line of defense: it computes a safe target of zero whenever temp_valid is false, no matter what the command frame asked for, then slew-limits the actual PWM by exactly one percent per 10-millisecond tick toward that target -- so the actuator never jumps instantly -- and it always returns true, because an output stage that reliably reaches a defined state is, by this design's own logic, healthy.
A design isn't done until you know how you'd prove it works on real hardware, with a real CAN adapter -- a PCAN-USB, a candleLight dongle, or a second S32K board -- actually on the bus.

display.heading: Bench-Test Plan
display.subheading: Proving every safety claim, not assuming it

beats.narration: You log the bus with candump and confirm 0x310 arrives every 100 milliseconds with its alive counter cycling 1 through 15 without skips. You send a cansend command with target 50 to request a 50 percent duty and watch PwmActualPct slew up over successive status frames. Then, the test that matters most: stop sending 0x311 entirely, and confirm PWM decays to zero within exactly 300 milliseconds of the last accepted command.

display.code:
# Bench test — CAN adapter (PCAN-USB / candleLight) on the bus

# 1. Status frame timing: confirm 0x310 every 100 ms, AliveCounter
#    incrementing 1 -> 15 -> 0 without skips
candump -t z

# 2. Command -> output: target 50% (0x32), alive nibble in low bits
#    of byte 1; watch PwmActualPct slew toward 50 over successive
#    0x310 frames
cansend can0 311#320F

# 3. Command timeout: stop sending 0x311 entirely
#    -> PWM must decay to 0% within 300 ms of the last accepted command

beats.narration: Two more steps close the loop: disconnect the thermistor and confirm SensorValid flips to zero within five samples, forcing PWM to zero regardless of the command; then, in a debug build, deliberately stall the sensor task for over 100 milliseconds and confirm the board actually resets, with the reset-cause register reporting watchdog -- not power-on. That's proof the supervision chain is really wired, not just present in the source.

display.heading: Fault Injection and Watchdog Proof
display.subheading: Six bench steps, each one a real safety claim

beats.narration: The cheat sheet distills it to one page: one 10-millisecond tick drives sensor, output, and watchdog, every tenth tick drives CAN transmit; command timeout is 300 milliseconds sharp; outputs are forced safe at boot and on any sensor or command fault; slew limiting caps actual PWM movement to one percent per tick; and the watchdog only gets fed when every task -- not just some -- reports healthy.

The lesson closes with an exercise, and it's not busywork -- it's the real skill this whole level was building toward. It asks you to write a one-page design note: the CAN table, the state diagram, and, most importantly, a known-limitations section that answers one uncomfortable question honestly.

display.heading: Exercise — and the Real Question
display.subheading: The design note every team writes before code review

beats.narration: Is there a race between the RX callback and the main loop reading g_cmd_target? Look back at the code: can_on_command_received can fire from a CAN interrupt at any point mid-tick, writing g_cmd_target and g_cmd_alive as plain globals with no lock, while command_watch_task_10ms reads them from the main loop. On a Cortex-M with aligned word writes that's often benign in practice -- but 'often benign' is not the same as 'proven safe,' and the lesson deliberately leaves that gap open. The second question is just as real: what happens if two nodes on the same bus get accidentally flashed with the same CAN ID? Answering both honestly, in writing, before anyone reviews your code, is the actual discipline this capstone is testing.

display.heading: The Race Condition
display.subheading: RX ISR vs. main-loop read of shared state -- no lock

beats.narration: This capstone is small enough to build in a weekend and honest enough to teach the real shape of automotive firmware: a fixed real-time schedule, a precisely specified bus protocol, a safe state that's genuine, not decorative, and a bench-test plan that proves every one of those claims instead of assuming them. From here, Level 2 picks up exactly where this capstone's rough edges are -- FlexCAN mailboxes, FreeRTOS, and UDS diagnostics -- to go close them properly.

display.heading: You've Reached the Capstone
display.subheading: One CAN sensor node, built to a real-time spec

beats.narration: Full lesson, the complete CAN layout tables, and every line of code shown here are at the link on screen -- go build it, then go find the race condition yourself.
